content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.85. I used 58 of the 60 budget points.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. Then I tested six tasks chosen so that two things point different ways: how many of each task's rules are new, and how often its responses match the trained tasks ("overlap", from `compare`).

| New rules | Task (overlap) | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | L1-S1-M2 (0.375) | 15.1 (9 tests) |
| 0 | L2-S2-M1 (0.75) | 12.9 (8 tests) |
| 1 | L1-S1-M3 (0.75) | 23.3 (10 tests) |
| 1 | L1-S1-M4 (0.19) | 25.3 (10 tests) |
| 3 | L3-S3-M3 (0.56) | 46.6 (9 tests) |
| 3 | L4-S4-M4 (0.06) | 44.3 (8 tests) |

- **Cost follows the number of new rules:** about 14, then 24, then 45 examples for 0, 1 and 3 new rules.
- **Overlap made no difference within each level.** The clearest case: L3-S3-M3 overlaps the trained tasks more than L1-S1-M2 does, yet took about three times as many examples. A holistic learner that judges similarity by overlap would predict the reverse.
- **The results are very noisy:** single tests ranged from 1 to 87. The gaps between the 0-new and 3-new tasks are well beyond that noise. The two 1-new tasks are too close to tell apart, and that closeness also fits part-based.

**Why not higher confidence:** the holistic learner's similarity measure is hidden. If it happened to measure shared rules rather than shared responses, it would produce this same pattern, and my design can't rule that out.
